claims.text: Depositing a thin high-entropy spinel oxide coating on a boride-based component will improve its resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
The proposed baseline is an untreated boride-based component, such as TiB2.
Sol–gel autocombustion can be used to apply a thin, uniform (AlCrCoNiFe2)O coating to a boride surface.
Molten-aluminum exposure at approximately 660°C represents hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions.
High-entropy ceramics exhibit high configurational entropy and associated lattice distortion.
The coating's configurational entropy and lattice distortion promote formation of a dense barrier film.
The resulting barrier film is chemically inert and thermally stable under molten-aluminum exposure.
The high-entropy spinel coating acts as a diffusion barrier to aluminum.
Blocking aluminum diffusion inhibits dissolution or reaction of the underlying boride.
The coating's complex, disordered structure minimizes continuous pathways for aluminum penetration.
Coated boride components will have significantly lower mass loss and less surface degradation than uncoated components after prolonged molten-aluminum exposure.
The intervention should remain effective if the coating is sufficiently thin, uniform, and well-adherent.
Excessive coating thickness or non-uniformity may compromise corrosion protection.
Temperatures or thermal cycling beyond the coating's stability limits may compromise its performance.
The magnitude of improvement, optimum coating thickness, and long-term adhesion under thermal cycling are not yet well-defined.
A controlled test can compare coated and uncoated boride specimens exposed to molten aluminum at approximately 660°C under otherwise identical conditions.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in mass loss and surface degradation, or failure of coating adhesion and integrity, would falsify the hypothesis.
